case_study_insert.main_stem: Rivermead Recycling Co-operative (RRC) is a cooperative in the recycling and waste-to-resource sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2015 by Ana Whitmore, the business turns council and commercial waste into biomass pellets and recycled aggregates, and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. RRC plans to invest $980,000 in a second pelletizing line at its Rivermead site, financed by $400,000 hire purchase of machinery and $580,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $640,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and currently produces 110,000 units a year. RRC faces two operational problems: contamination of incoming sorted waste has averaged 6.4%, and absenteeism has reached 11%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2026: The plant processed 27,500 units last quarter; contamination averaged 6.4%, down from 7.9% a year ago. Complaints from council customers fell from 17 to 9 per month. Average waste-to-pellet turnaround is 2.8 days. Fourteen near-miss incidents were logged; 18 of 60 staff have not completed machine-safety refresher training at $650 per employee. The household recycling rate in RRC's catchment stands at 44%, up from 39%.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Rivermead Recycling Co-operative for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25% in September 2026, increasing borrowing costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $12.30 to $13.10 per hour from April 2027, raising sorting and pelletizing payroll costs. (3) The landfill tax will increase by 14.0% to $126 a tonne from April 2027, making waste-to-resource recovery cheaper than landfill; business waste collections grew 3.4% in the same period.

questions.question_text: RRC plans to finance part of the second pelletizing line with hire purchase and retained profit. Explain two advantages for RRC of using hire purchase rather than a bank loan to buy the new machinery.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase lets RRC spread the $400,000 cost of the pelletizing machinery over its working life in fixed monthly instalments instead of drawing a lump-sum bank loan, protecting cash flow for the $580,000 retained-profit slice and everyday operations such as council gate-fee billing and waste haulage. Payments are known in advance, which makes budgeting for the 110,000-unit output and the 11% absenteeism problem far easier than variable loan repayments.

Point 2: With hire purchase the machinery is used from day one and ownership transfers after the final payment, so RRC acquires a productive second line without the collateral demands, early-repayment penalties or personal guarantees a bank might impose on a cooperative whose members trade with limited capital. If council contracts win, the machine pays for itself out of revenue; if not, RRC has limited its exposure to the instalments paid plus the machine itself, rather than a secured loan against the whole site.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Rivermead Recycling Co-operative and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: RRC is launching its recycled-aggregate brand to councils and builders. Consider local radio sponsorship, a trade newsletter sent to council procurement officers, or a community social-media campaign about zero-waste living. Which should RRC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local radio sponsorship: A sponsorship of the morning traffic show on regional stations would build name recognition among households (the 44% household recycling rate up from 39% shows growing public interest), but listeners are mostly private individuals, not tender-evaluating procurement officers, and coverage cannot be bought for only the two districts where RRC's customers operate. Cost per qualified B2B lead is poor.

Trade newsletter to council procurement officers: A targeted slot in a council procurement newsletter reaches exactly the people who sign waste-to-resource contracts, can feature the 6.4% contamination improvement, the 2.8-day turnaround and complaints falling from 17 to 9 per month, and costs only a few hundred dollars per insertion with measurable response. Reach is narrow and frequency limited, so awareness among the wider builder market would remain low.

Community social-media campaign: A zero-waste campaign on community Facebook groups and Instagram would build public goodwill, pressure councils to award RRC contracts, and appeal to environmentally conscious builders for its recycled aggregates. It is nearly free but results are indirect and slow; it rarely produces contract signatures within a quarter and needs constant content production.

Recommendation: RRC should choose the trade newsletter to council procurement officers. Waste-to-resource revenue comes from council and commercial contracts, so reaching decision-makers directly yields the fastest, cheapest route to orders; radio and social media build awareness but not tenders. Radio is rejected as untargeted and cost-ineffective for B2B; the social campaign is rejected as too slow and indirect to carry a commercial launch, though it should continue as a supporting activity for community goodwill.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of RRC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of RRC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and social media are rejected as primary channels.

questions.question_text: RRC's absenteeism has reached 11% and contamination of incoming sorted waste has averaged 6.4%. Explain two benefits for RRC of its democratic leadership and flat structure.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 60 member-employees a genuine voice in how the sorting line is organised — shift patterns, contamination checks and safety briefings — which satisfies social and esteem needs (Maslow) and strengthens Herzberg's motivation factors of involvement and recognition. Workers who helped design the new contamination-flagging routine are more likely to follow it consistently, directly attacking the 6.4% average that forces reject loads, rework cost and extra $650 refresher training for 18 uncertified staff.

Point 2: A flat structure shortens the chain of command, so an absence spike reaches Ana Whitmore's management group the same shift and cover can be rearranged without a management layer; informal peer communication also means safety near-misses are flagged quickly. It reinforces cooperative values of equality and shared responsibility, lowering the turnover and disengagement that typically drive 11% absenteeism, and it keeps overhead inside the $640,000 fixed costs while the $980,000 second pelletizing line beds in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RRC's absenteeism, contamination and cooperative structure.

questions.question_text: RRC wants to improve productivity on the sorting line without raising contamination. Consider performance-related piece-rate pay or team working for its sorters. Which should RRC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Piece-rate pay: Paying sorters per tonne processed would directly reward output, suiting Taylor-style scientific management, and could lift volumes toward what the new $980,000 pelletizing line needs to run at capacity. It is simple to administer and feels immediately rewarding. However, sorters rushing for money will miss contaminants, the 6.4% contamination rate would likely rise, reject loads would cost councils' trust (complaints fell from 17 to 9 per month), and safety near-misses (14 were logged) would increase as speed trumps care. It also conflicts with RRC's cooperative ethos of equal sharing.

Team working: Grouping sorters into small teams with shared quality and safety targets builds social belonging and shared ownership — the very motivators that sit behind RRC's democratic leadership and cooperative ethos — satisfying esteem needs and tapping Herzberg's motivators of teamwork and responsibility. Teams can run quality circles to attack contamination at its source, watch each other's near-misses and cover absences mutually — crucial with absenteeism at 11%. Drawbacks: pay is not immediately tied to output, some strong performers may resent free-riders, and team bonus administration is more complex.

Decision: RRC should choose team working. It directly supports the two problems identified — 6.4% contamination (through shared quality ownership and peer checking of loads) and 11% absenteeism (through peer support and belonging) — while fitting cooperative culture and protecting the council contracts that took years to win; team meetings can be slotted into shift changeovers so output is protected. Piece-rate pay is rejected because it incentivises raw speed over quality and safety, would likely push contamination and injuries upward, disadvantages newer sorters, and conflicts with the cooperative's equal-share principles; crucially, it does nothing to address why people are absent.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivation methods with limited application to RRC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both motivation methods in the context of RRC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both motivation methods in the context of RRC with a well-justified decision covering quality, safety, culture and absenteeism.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how RRC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $640,000 ÷ ($20.00 − $12.00) = $640,000 ÷ $8.00 = 80,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 80,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $20.00 − $12.00 = $8.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $8.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways RRC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. RRC's managers can compare the 80,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 110,000 units to confirm expansion economics, with a margin of safety of 30,000 units, informing whether the new pelletizing line can reach full utilisation.
2. Contribution per unit of $8.00 lets RRC model council tender pricing: for example, a contract priced at $18.00 cuts contribution to $6.00, so managers can check the guaranteed volume still covers the $640,000 fixed costs before signing.
3. The unit cost of $17.82 a unit ($1,960,000 total costs ÷ 110,000 units) can be benchmarked quarter by quarter to expose contamination reject waste, renegotiate haulage and fuel supply against the 5.25% interest environment and rising input costs, and set tariff levels.
4. Knowing break-even output helps managers set shift rotas that cover the 11% absenteeism without breaching delivery promises (2.8 days turnaround), and to check the $400,000 hire purchase instalments can be serviced from the $8.00 unit contribution on 30,000 excess units.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 80,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $8.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 30,000 units; tender modelling at $8.00 contribution; unit cost benchmarking at $17.82 to attack contamination waste; and hire-purchase servicing checks on the $980,000 expansion.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RRC's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has RRC's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 34.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 38.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 20.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 22.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.5%
ROCE 2025 = 22.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $1,850,000 revenue − $1,221,000 cost of sales = $629,000; 2025 gross profit = $2,200,000 revenue − $1,364,000 cost of sales = $836,000. Operating profit rose from $370,000 to $484,000. Capital employed rose from $2,000,000 to $2,200,000. 2024: $629,000 ÷ $1,850,000 = 34.0%; $370,000 ÷ $1,850,000 = 20.0%; $370,000 ÷ $2,000,000 = 18.5%. 2025: $836,000 ÷ $2,200,000 = 38.0%; $484,000 ÷ $2,200,000 = 22.0%; $484,000 ÷ $2,200,000 = 22.0%.

Evaluation: Performance has clearly improved. Revenue grew 18.9% to $2,200,000 while productivity and contamination gains (6.4%, down from 7.9%) lifted gross profit by $207,000 with no proportionate rise in costs of sales — evidence the turnaround and better feedstock segregation are working. The gains sit after interest payable rose from $95,000 to $125,000 and after the extra $1,364,000 cost-of-sales base, so the expansion pipeline is contributing genuinely, not cosmetically. Residual risks: the September rate rise to 5.25% will lift finance costs further, landfill-tax passthrough depends on council negotiations, and a single contaminated batch can erase weeks of margin.

Conclusion: RRC's financial performance has improved. Revenue, gross profit, operating profit and every return measure (34.0% to 38.0%, 20.0% to 22.0%, 18.5% to 22.0%) moved upward with capital employed broadly flat, so returns per dollar of investment improved. The cooperative must lock in council contract renewals and hold the contamination gains to sustain them.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, operating profit and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether RRC's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RRC of the 14.0% landfill-tax increase taking effect in April 2027.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The landfill tax rise to $126 a tonne makes dumping waste far more expensive for councils and builders, channelling more material into waste-to-resource recovery. RRC's feedstock volumes would grow without extra marketing spend, helping fill the second pelletizing line's capacity, and RRC can charge competitive gate fees knowing landfill is the scarce alternative — reinforcing the 44% household recycling rate and the 3.4% growth in business waste collections.

Disadvantage: A larger flow of waste does not guarantee cleaner loads — contamination (already 6.4%) may worsen as councils push marginal material onto recyclers to dodge the new $126 a tonne landfill tax, raising reject and re-sorting costs and risking the complaints record RRC fought to cut from 17 to 9 per month. Council budget pressure could also squeeze the gate fees RRC hopes to raise, thinning the $20.00 selling price and ultimately the $8.00 contribution per unit if RRC enters a price war with larger landfill-reliant incumbents who can subsidise gate fees from other divisions.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RRC's waste economics and operations.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the landfill tax rise to $126 a tonne will affect RRC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): RRC's hire-purchase instalments are usually fixed, so the immediate cash effect is small — about $3,000 a year if any variable borrowing exists. But the 0.75-point rise increases the cost of future borrowing for the Rivermead expansion, may cool construction activity that generates RRC's feedstock, and lifts council budgeting stress, indirectly tightening gate-fee negotiations. The direct financial hit is the smallest of the three.

Minimum wage rise (6.5%, to $13.10 per hour from April 2027): With 60 mainly sorting and pelletizing staff on hourly pay, the award adds about $0.80 per hour; at around 2,000 hours a year that is roughly $1,600 per worker or about $96,000 a year — close to 20% of operating profit. Combined with 11% absenteeism already forcing overtime, the payroll pressure is substantial, though mechanisation of the new line should claw some back through labour productivity.

Landfill tax rise (14.0%, to $126 a tonne from April 2027): This is market-shaping rather than cost-side. Every tonne diverted from landfill to RRC strengthens its pipeline at zero marketing cost; councils facing a $126-per-tonne alternative will pay RRC's gate fees, directly supporting the 3.4% growth in business waste collections and RRC's 44% catchment recycling rate. It also enables RRC to renegotiate multi-year council contracts at better prices. The risk is contamination rising with volumes.

Conclusion: The landfill tax rise will have the greatest impact. It is the only one of the three that expands RRC's market and revenue, not merely its costs; it reshapes council behaviour in RRC's favour for years, outweighing the ~$96,000 wage award and the negligible rate effect. The wage increase is second in cash terms, the interest rise is smallest and can be managed by fixing HP terms; all three still require RRC to invest in contamination control and mechanisation.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to RRC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on RRC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of RRC with a well-justified judgement that the landfill-tax rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
